strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically appealing alternative to per-scene semantic feature optimization for 3DGS: lift tracked 2D masks into Gaussian groups, refine ambiguous boundary points, and perform open-vocabulary matching through VLM-derived textual descriptions. The training-free framing is useful for deployment if the reported efficiency holds.

The empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks. On LERF object selection, the method reaches 54.3 mean mIoU, above both point-based and pixel-based baselines, and on ScanNet it consistently improves over OpenGaussian, InstanceGaussian, and Dr.Splat across 19/15/10-class settings.

The ablations support the two main design choices: neutral point processing improves LERF mIoU from 53.0 to 54.3, and VLM-text matching substantially outperforms single-view, averaged, and filtered CLIP image matching. These experiments make the claimed benefit of semantic distillation more credible.

The method targets real limitations of existing 3DGS language methods: high per-scene optimization cost, large feature storage, and cross-view CLIP feature instability. The reported storage reduction from roughly 3GB to 3MB and lower peak VRAM are potentially valuable.
The manuscript is generally readable, with a coherent pipeline and useful qualitative comparisons illustrating boundary quality and failure modes of feature-matching baselines.
weaknesses: The central polysemy claim is not convincingly evaluated. The method can attach multiple VLM-generated names to an object group, but there is no dedicated benchmark or analysis showing that the same Gaussian can reliably support overlapping concepts such as object category, material, part, affordance, and superclass. Most reported metrics are standard single-label object or class segmentation.

Reproducibility is weak in several important places. The exact VLM prompt, top-N key-view value, similarity threshold eta, entropy/opacity thresholds, periodic detection interval, IoU criterion for new objects, and full scene/category splits are not specified. Since these parameters can materially affect grouping and matching, fixed-threshold claims are hard to verify.

The reliance on Gemini 2.5 Pro introduces a proprietary, stochastic component whose versioning, decoding settings, cost, latency, and failure behavior are not reported. This makes the training-free claim practically less clean and complicates fair comparison with methods that do not use a closed VLM at inference time.

The efficiency comparison is incomplete. Table 1 reports training time, feature storage, and peak VRAM, but not total preprocessing/inference time for SAM multi-granularity segmentation, DAM2SAM tracking, back-projection over masks/views/Gaussians, rendering for evaluation, or VLM calls. The claim of reducing scene adaptation from hours to minutes is therefore not fully substantiated.

The evaluation scope is somewhat narrow for the breadth of claims. LERF has only four scenes, and the ScanNet protocol is summarized but not detailed enough to assess difficulty, scene selection, and whether class-name matching via generated text is robust across diverse indoor environments.

The comparison may not be fully controlled. The method uses strong external components, including SAM, DAM2SAM, CLIP text encoding, and Gemini, while baselines may use different masks, feature extraction pipelines, or optimization assumptions. The paper would benefit from a clearer accounting of which inputs and pretrained models are shared across methods.

The object grouping method depends heavily on initial 2D mask quality and tracking. The limitation is acknowledged, but the paper does not quantify sensitivity to segmentation/tracking failures, occlusion, small objects, transparent objects, or cases where a SAM mask corresponds to a part rather than an instance.

Some technical details are under-specified. The back-projection aggregation over all intersected Gaussians could be expensive, but implementation details such as visibility pruning, rasterization reuse, numerical thresholds, and handling overlapping masks at multiple granularities are not described.

The ScanNet setup disables 3D Gaussian densification to align with ground-truth point clouds, which may change the underlying 3DGS representation and limit comparability with normal 3DGS pipelines. The effect of this choice on rendering quality and segmentation accuracy is not analyzed.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially that downstream modules gracefully handle data preparation artifacts and that the framework is VLM-agnostic. Only one VLM is evaluated, and no robustness analysis supports these broader statements.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: avoiding costly per-scene semantic optimization for open-vocabulary understanding in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually simple and potentially useful: lift multi-view segmentation masks into 3D object groups, remove ambiguous boundary Gaussians, and use language-side matching for object retrieval.

The reported results are promising on the included benchmarks, with gains over several 3DGS open-vocabulary baselines on LERF object selection and ScanNet semantic segmentation, while also reporting lower storage and VRAM usage.
The ablations in Tables 4 and 5 provide some evidence that the VLM-based text distillation contributes substantially over direct CLIP image-feature aggregation.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited. The method largely combines existing components: SAM/DAM2SAM tracking, mask back-projection, entropy/opacity filtering, Gemini-based object naming, and CLIP text matching. The paper does not convincingly establish a new technical principle beyond this engineering composition.

The central claim of being polysemy-aware is weakly supported. The method assigns object-level textual candidate names to groups and unions matched groups. There is no explicit per-Gaussian multi-label representation, no benchmark for polysemous queries, and no evaluation showing that points can correctly support multiple simultaneous semantic concepts such as material, part, affordance, and category.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. LERF contains only four scenes in Table 2, and the paper does not report variance, per-query breakdowns, failure cases, or robustness to tracking/segmentation errors. The ScanNet evaluation description omits the exact scene list and details needed to judge whether comparisons are fully matched.

The comparison may be unfair because the proposed method uses Gemini 2.5 Pro to generate object names, while several baselines rely on CLIP image features or learned scene features. The benefit may come from a much stronger external VLM rather than the proposed 3D method. There is no controlled comparison using the same VLM for baselines or simpler alternatives such as VLM captioning plus 2D mask tracking.

Important implementation details are missing, harming reproducibility: the VLM prompt, top-N view count, similarity threshold eta, entropy and opacity thresholds, periodic detection interval, IoU threshold for new instances, SAM/DAM2SAM settings, CLIP model variant, and runtime including VLM calls are not specified.

The technical justification for neutral point processing is underdeveloped. The assumption that high entropy plus low opacity identifies semantically neutral boundary points is plausible but not rigorously validated; the ablation shows only a small gain from this module, from 53.0 to 54.3 mIoU.

The method remains heavily dependent on 2D segmentation and tracking quality, despite claiming downstream robustness. The limitations acknowledge SAM and VLM errors, but the experiments do not stress-test these dependencies or quantify sensitivity to mask noise, missed tracks, distractors, or incorrect VLM labels.

Several claims are overstated. The paper says it uses uncompressed CLIP representations for linguistic precision, but the main matching representation is generated text encoded by CLIP, not preserved image features. It also claims SOTA-level performance and robust inconsistency reconciliation without sufficient breadth or controlled evidence.

Efficiency claims are incomplete. Table 1 reports storage and VRAM but not total wall-clock time including SAM mask generation, DAM2SAM tracking, rendering/back-projection, and Gemini API inference. The “training-free” framing is useful but does not by itself establish practical speed without full pipeline timing.

Presentation clarity is acceptable at a high level, but key experimental protocol details are absent, and some descriptions are imprecise or contradictory, such as listing Dr.Splat as having no scene optimization while still reporting around one hour of train time.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck in open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian Splatting: per-scene semantic optimization. A training-free matching pipeline with 2D mask lifting, neutral-point filtering, and VLM-based instance naming is a useful and timely alternative to feature-learning approaches.

The empirical results are strong relative to the included baselines. The method reports the best mean mIoU on LERF object selection and ScanNet semantic segmentation, while also substantially reducing stated memory/storage and eliminating scene-specific semantic training.

The core design is conceptually simple and plausible: probabilistic mask back-projection gives 3D object groups, entropy plus opacity addresses boundary ambiguity, and VLM text distillation is a reasonable way to reduce multi-view CLIP image-feature inconsistency.

The ablations support the two main components. Neutral point processing improves LERF mIoU from 53.0 to 54.3, and VLM-text matching substantially outperforms single-view, averaged, and filtered CLIP image matching.
The method has clear potential usefulness for interactive 3D scene querying, because it operates directly on Gaussian points and appears much lighter than prior optimization-heavy pipelines.
weaknesses: The strongest novelty claim, polysemous representation, is not convincingly evaluated. The experiments mostly test object/class selection and segmentation; there is no focused benchmark or analysis showing that a single Gaussian/object can reliably support multiple simultaneous concepts such as part, material, function, and category better than alternatives.

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on Gemini 2.5 Pro for semantic distillation. The exact prompts, top-N view selection details, candidate-name format, thresholds, API settings, randomness control, and failure handling are not specified enough to reproduce the reported numbers. A proprietary VLM also complicates fair comparison and long-term reproducibility.

The evaluation breadth is somewhat limited. LERF has few scenes, and ScanNet results are summarized over selected 19/15/10 class settings without enough detail on scene splits, number of scenes, category selection, or statistical variation. The paper would be stronger with broader datasets and per-scene variance or confidence intervals.

The efficiency comparison is incomplete. The table emphasizes no training and small CLIP feature storage, but the full wall-clock cost of SAM/DAM2SAM mask generation, periodic re-segmentation, VLM calls, and per-object processing is not clearly reported. Since the method shifts cost from optimization to segmentation/tracking/VLM inference, end-to-end runtime is important.

Several technical choices are underspecified or potentially fragile: entropy uses projected Gaussian centers rather than rendered contribution distributions, visibility handling is unclear, fixed entropy/opacity thresholds are not reported in the extracted method text, and the claim that downstream modules gracefully handle tracking/re-identification errors is not experimentally validated.

The VLM naming stage may introduce semantic hallucinations or collapse fine-grained visual evidence into coarse labels. The limitation is acknowledged, but there is little quantitative analysis of VLM errors, alternative VLMs, prompt sensitivity, or how often incorrect object names dominate final retrieval.

Some baselines and comparisons need more care. The manuscript compares against many recent methods, but does not clearly state whether results are reproduced under identical 3DGS reconstructions, mask generators, queries, and thresholds. Some cited related work on view-dependent semantics appears relevant but is not experimentally compared.

Presentation is generally understandable, but some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially statements of SOTA-level performance and robustness. More implementation detail, clearer task definitions, and fuller reporting of hyperparameters would improve scientific clarity.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: open-vocabulary understanding for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes with lower storage and adaptation cost than feature-embedding approaches.

The central idea of decoupling geometry from semantics via an extrinsic object-index layer is intuitive and useful. Representing object groups separately from Gaussian parameters avoids storing high-dimensional per-Gaussian features and naturally supports overlapping/multi-granularity semantic groups.

The method is computationally attractive. The reported LERF efficiency comparison shows no per-scene optimization, about 3 MB CLIP feature storage versus about 3 GB for many embedding baselines, and lower peak VRAM. The supplementary runtime breakdown is also helpful.

The paper provides evaluations on two relevant settings, LERF open-vocabulary object selection and ScanNet semantic segmentation, with comparisons to several recent 3DGS language-understanding baselines.

The ablations are meaningful: the paper isolates neutral point processing, VLM/text-based feature extraction versus CLIP image feature aggregation, VLM choice, number of generated nouns, sparse mask supervision, and threshold sensitivity.

The qualitative examples and failure-case analysis help clarify where the method succeeds: sharper object boundaries, better part/object separation in some scenes, and failures caused by inaccurate masks or VLM mislabeling.
weaknesses: A major concern is that the claimed state-of-the-art performance is not supported by the paper’s own LERF table. Table 2 reports Ours at 54.3 mean mIoU, below Occam’s LGS at 61.3, 3DVLGS at 62.0, and LAGA at 64.0. The text nevertheless claims a new SOTA result and a 3.9 mIoU improvement over the previous best. This is a material correctness/presentation issue because it affects the main empirical claim.

The method relies heavily on powerful external components, especially Gemini 2.5 Pro for naming instances, SAM, and DAM2SAM. The contribution over simply obtaining good object tracks and asking a strong VLM to name highlighted objects is therefore not fully disentangled. The VLM ablation shows performance varies substantially by VLM, making the method’s gains partly attributable to the proprietary recognizer rather than the proposed 3D representation.

Reproducibility is limited. Gemini 2.5 Pro is closed/proprietary and may change over time; the paper does not fully specify API settings, determinism, cost, rate constraints, or how generated nouns are handled when outputs are inconsistent. This is important because the semantic index is produced by this model.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness questions. Some baselines use CLIP image embeddings or learned 3D features, while the proposed method uses a much stronger modern VLM to convert images into textual object names. Without giving baselines access to comparable VLM-based semantic naming, the accuracy comparison may conflate representation design with semantic recognizer strength.

The evidence for the proposed neutral point mechanism is modest. The main ablation improves LERF mIoU from 53.0 to 54.3, and the threshold study varies within a narrow range. This supports a small refinement but does not strongly validate neutral points as a major technical contribution.

The open-vocabulary claim is somewhat constrained by the noun-list matching design. Each object is represented by five generated nouns and matched by CLIP text similarity with a fixed threshold. This may work for common object categories but is less convincing for attributes, affordances, relations, fine-grained descriptions, or compositional queries, which are central to open-vocabulary understanding.

The paper does not sufficiently evaluate robustness to segmentation/tracking failures even though the pipeline depends on SAM/DAM2SAM masks. The appendix argues that missing or duplicate tracks are handled gracefully, but the main evidence is mostly qualitative or sparse-mask experiments rather than systematic stress tests with corrupted masks, occlusions, dynamic scenes, or tracking identity switches.

The storage/runtime comparison may be incomplete because it emphasizes CLIP feature storage while not fully accounting for all extrinsic index data, mask tracks, object-to-Gaussian memberships, VLM inference cost, and any API latency/cost. The paper reports a useful runtime breakdown, but the headline efficiency claims should be qualified more carefully.

Several claims are overstated: phrases such as 'guarantees precise semantics', 'more efficient and semantically robust foundation', and broad claims of outperforming embedding-based frameworks exceed what the reported mixed results demonstrate.

The experiments are limited in breadth for a CVPR-level claim. LERF has only four scenes in the reported table, ScanNet uses the same 10 scenes as OpenGaussian, and real-world/Grasp-Net results are qualitative. More datasets, unseen categories, and stronger statistical reporting would be needed for a convincing acceptance case.

strengths: The paper identifies a real limitation of per-Gaussian semantic feature embedding: it can be storage-heavy, view-dependent, and awkward for object/part polysemy. The proposed object-group plus semantic-index framing is a reasonable direction for open-vocabulary 3DGS understanding.

The pipeline is practically motivated and combines multi-view masks, 3D back-projection, neutral/boundary point filtering, and VLM-generated textual hypotheses into a simple query mechanism. This could be useful for interactive scene selection/editing when high-quality masks and VLM labels are available.

The manuscript includes several relevant comparisons and ablations. The ScanNet table reports consistent gains over the listed 3D baselines, and the runtime breakdown in the supplement gives some useful detail about bottlenecks such as VLM inference, mask acquisition, and backward matching.

The supplementary material provides concrete implementation choices, including mask tracking intervals, thresholds, prompt format, number of VLM nouns, and similarity threshold, which helps partially assess reproducibility.
weaknesses: A central quantitative claim is not supported by the paper's own results. The manuscript states that the method achieves a new SOTA on LERF and outperforms the previous best by 3.9 mIoU, but Table 2 reports a mean mIoU of 54.3 for the method, below Occam's LGS at 61.3, 3DVLGS at 62.0, and LAGA at 64.0. This is not a minor presentation issue; it materially misrepresents the evidence.

The contribution appears more like a pipeline composition than a clearly novel technical advance. SAM/DAM2SAM masks, mask back-projection into 3DGS, CLIP text matching, and VLM naming are combined sensibly, but the paper does not convincingly isolate what is fundamentally new beyond the extrinsic-index framing and a simple entropy/opacity boundary filter.

The neutral point mechanism is overclaimed relative to the evidence. In Table 4 it improves LERF mIoU from 53.0 to 54.3, and the threshold ablation peaks only slightly above nearby settings. This does not substantiate strong claims that neutral point handling is a major reason for semantic clarity or boundary accuracy.

The efficiency claims are potentially misleading. Table 1 lists no scene optimization or training time for the proposed method and emphasizes only about 3 MB of CLIP feature storage, but the supplement reports about 9.25 minutes per LERF scene including mask acquisition, backward matching, and VLM text acquisition. The storage accounting also appears to omit or under-discuss object masks/tracks, group membership indices, and external VLM dependence.

Reproducibility is weak because the best results rely on Gemini 2.5 Pro, a closed and changing VLM. The ablation shows a large drop with other VLMs, so the method's performance is substantially tied to an external proprietary model rather than the proposed algorithm alone.

The evaluation is narrow and uneven. LERF uses only four scenes, ScanNet uses the same ten scenes as prior work, and the additional real-world/GraspNet results are qualitative. There is no strong test of robustness under mask failures, VLM label errors, prompt variation, similarity-threshold variation, or more diverse open-vocabulary queries.

The comparison protocol raises fairness concerns. The method uses powerful VLM-based object naming while many baselines use CLIP image embeddings or learned per-point features; the paper does not adequately separate gains from stronger semantic priors in the VLM versus gains from the proposed 3D representation.

Some claims are too absolute: phrases such as guarantees precise semantics, gracefully handles tracking/re-identification errors, and several orders of magnitude storage reduction are not fully justified by the experiments. The stated robustness to duplicated or missing tracks is argued conceptually but not quantitatively validated.

Important ablations are missing. The paper does not clearly ablate multi-granularity grouping, overlapping membership, number of selected views, query threshold eta, mask tracker quality, SAM granularity choices, or replacing VLM nouns with ground-truth/category names to measure how much performance comes from recognition versus grouping.

Clarity is generally acceptable, but the writing repeatedly overstates conclusions. A more accurate manuscript would distinguish training-free indexing from total scene adaptation cost, report SOTA only within the relevant subset if applicable, and state limitations of mask/VLM dependence more plainly.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful shift from per-Gaussian semantic feature embedding to an extrinsic object/group index. This is technically well motivated: object-level grouping, overlapping multi-granularity groups, and textual hypotheses directly address storage bloat, point/object semantic mismatch, and polysemy in existing 3DGS language methods.

The method is appealingly practical: it is training-free after the 3DGS reconstruction, avoids per-scene semantic optimization, and reports large efficiency gains. The reported resource table and runtime breakdown support the claim that the approach can reduce feature storage and adaptation time substantially compared with optimization-heavy embedding methods.

Experimental evidence is reasonably broad for this area, covering LERF object selection and ScanNet open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation, with comparisons to many recent baselines. The ScanNet results are particularly strong, with consistent gains over OpenGaussian, InstanceGaussian, Dr.Splat, LAGA, and LUDVIG across 19/15/10 class settings.

The ablations are useful and targeted. The paper separately studies neutral point processing, VLM/text-based feature extraction versus CLIP-image aggregation, VLM choice, prompt count, and neutral-point thresholds, which helps identify which parts of the pipeline matter.

The paper is generally clear and well structured. The supplementary material gives concrete implementation details, thresholds, prompts, scene lists, failure cases, and a component-wise runtime analysis, improving reproducibility relative to many papers in this space.
weaknesses: The strongest accuracy claim is overstated for LERF. Table 2 shows the proposed method at 54.3 mean mIoU, below several listed methods such as LAGA at 64.0, 3DVLGS at 62.0, and Occam’s LGS at 61.3. The method is competitive among some 3D/training-free settings, but the manuscript’s statement of a new SOTA result on this benchmark is not supported by its own table.

The approach depends heavily on external foundation models, especially Gemini 2.5 Pro for object naming and SAM/DAM2SAM for masks/tracking. This raises reproducibility and stability concerns: Gemini is proprietary, prompts/API behavior may change, and the reported performance varies notably with VLM choice. The method’s contribution is therefore partly a pipeline composition whose quality may track external VLM improvements rather than a fully controlled algorithmic advance.

The evaluation breadth is still limited. ScanNet uses only the 10 scenes from OpenGaussian, LERF has limited scene/query diversity, and the additional real-world and Grasp-Net experiments are qualitative. For a method positioned as a robust paradigm shift, more datasets, larger-scale quantitative tests, and failure-rate analysis under mask/tracking degradation would strengthen the evidence.

Fairness of efficiency comparisons is somewhat unclear. The reported storage comparison emphasizes CLIP feature storage, but the full footprint of masks, object groups, indices, generated text hypotheses, and possible VLM/API costs is not fully accounted for. Runtime also includes VLM text acquisition but does not clearly discuss remote inference variability or cost.

The neutral point concept is intuitive and useful, but the technical formulation is relatively heuristic, relying on fixed entropy and opacity thresholds. Ablations show modest gains on LERF, but there is limited evidence that these thresholds transfer broadly or that neutral points are the decisive factor behind the main performance improvements.

The query mechanism appears limited to matching user text against a small set of VLM-generated nouns with a fixed CLIP similarity threshold. This may work well for category/object names, but it is less clear how robustly the system handles compositional, relational, attribute-heavy, or rare queries, despite the paper’s broader open-vocabulary framing.
